International guidelines7 have recommended starting intravenous anti- bacterial therapy as early as possible, and within the first hour of recognition of septic shock; the initial choice of therapy should be broad enough to cover all likely patho- gens, and it should be reassessed daily to optimise activity and prevent the development of resistance. De-escalation of combination therapy to the most appropriate single ther- apy should be carried out as soon as susceptibility of the infection is known. The typical duration of therapy will be 7 to 10 days. Empirical treatment has often begun with a penicillin and an aminoglycoside, metronidazole being added if anaerobic infection is suspected. In the UK, the BNF recommends that initial empirical treatment for com- munity-acquired septicaemia is with either a broad-spec- trum antipseudomonal penicillin (such as ticarcillin-clavu- lanic acid or piperacillin-tazobactam) or a broad-spectrum cephalosporin (such as ceftazidime or cefotaxime); for hospital-acquired septicaemia a broad-spectrum antipseu- domonal beta-lactam antibacterial (such as ceftazidime, ticarcillin-clavulanic acid, piperacillin-tazobactam, imi- penem-cilastatin, or meropenem) is recommended. In both cases, an aminoglycoside should be added if Pseu- domonas is suspected or if sepsis is severe, metronidazole if anaerobic organisms are suspected, and vancomycin (or teicoplanin) if meticillin-resistant staphylococci are sus- pected. US guidelines8 recommend a third- or fourth-gen- eration cephalosporin (cefotaxime, ceftriaxone, ceftazi- dime, or cefepime), or piperacillin-tazobactam, or imipenem-cilastatin, or meropenem, in each case with an aminoglycoside (gentamicin, tobramycin, or amikacin) for the initial treatment of life-threatening sepsis in adults. When there is some information on which to base choice of treatment, but before the infecting organisms are defi- nitely known, the following treatment is suggested: • suspected bacterial endocarditis—ceftriaxone with van- comycin, possibly with gentamicin as well • suspected meticillin-resistant staphylococci—vanco- mycin, alone or with gentamicin and/or rifampicin Once the infecting organisms have been identified, choice of treatment will again depend on their sensitivity and cur- rent patterns of resistance in the community or hospital.
